content.text: {"persuasion":"UNPERSUADED","support_scope":"NONE","rationale":"The cited texts support a strong association among God's Name, his temple, the ark, covenant, authority, and household belonging, but they do not establish that “Name” means the covenant identity of a house or that it is constituted specifically by manna/Word, covenant law, and fruitful priesthood. The strongest counter-reading—Name as the identity, presence, honor, and authority of its bearer—explains the temple and marriage texts more directly. A house is built for God's Name because it is dedicated to and represents God; the ark is placed there as the locus of his covenantal presence. Hebrews 9:4 inventories the ark, but neither it nor the related passages identify that inventory as the semantic constituents of the Name. The entry's claims about counterfeit Names and taking the Name in vain therefore depend on an unestablished constitutive inference.","book_core_identification":"A Name is the covenant identity of a house, constituted by its Head's Word, covenant law, and fruitful priesthood.","book_secondary_elaborations":["Substituting any one of the three constituents creates a counterfeit Name.","Rejecting, replacing, or removing any one of the three constituents takes the Name in vain."],"unsupported_glossary_assertions":["That “Name” specifically denotes the covenant identity of a house rather than principally the identity, presence, honor, or authority of the named bearer.","That the Head's Word, covenant law, and fruitful priesthood are the three constitutive elements of a Name.","That substituting any one of those elements necessarily creates a counterfeit Name.","That rejecting, replacing, or removing any one of those elements is what it means to take the Name in vain."],"chapter_only_objections":["The identification of every prayer made “in Jesus' Name” with acting specifically within the proposed Word-covenant-priesthood triad goes beyond the glossary entry.","The detailed mapping of the Lord's Prayer onto manna, covenant law, and priestly intercession is a chapter-level typological application.","The interpretation of the seven women retaining their own bread and apparel as rejecting the proposed threefold substance of the Name exceeds what Isaiah 4:1 itself establishes.","The application of the triad to Babel, the beast's name, the Father's name on foreheads, and Acts 4:12 is chapter-only and requires separate evaluation."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"In the supplied passages, a name represents and publicly identifies its bearer—especially the bearer's identity, presence, ownership, honor, and authority. A house built “for the name of the LORD” is a sanctuary dedicated to God and associated with his covenantal presence; the ark belongs there as the covenantal locus of that presence. Being called by a man's name signifies marital or household affiliation. The ark's contents express aspects of Israel's covenant with God, but they do not constitute a lexical or symbolic definition of “Name.”","counter_core_identification":"Name signifies the identity and represented presence or authority of its bearer, with household belonging arising when that name is placed upon a house or people.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter denies that a Name is inherently the covenant identity of a house or that its substance consists of the ark's three listed contents; the house and ark bear or represent God's Name rather than define what Name means.","counter_case":["Second Samuel 6:2 explicitly identifies the relevant name as “the name of the LORD of hosts,” naturally making the LORD the bearer and referent of the Name; the ark is the place over which that Name is called and where the LORD is represented as dwelling.","Second Samuel 7:13 and 1 Kings 8:20 describe a house built “for” God's Name, which naturally means a sanctuary dedicated to and representing God, not that Name itself means the house's covenant identity.","First Kings 8:21 explains why the ark belongs in the sanctuary: it contains the covenant. It does not say that the ark or its contents constitute the Name.","Hebrews 9:4 supplies an inventory of the ark. The subsequent equations—manna as the Head's Word and Aaron's rod as fruitful priesthood—are typological constructions, not stated definitions of Name.","Deuteronomy 8:3 says the manna taught dependence upon God's spoken word; it does not identify manna itself as one constituent of a Name.","Deuteronomy 4:13 directly supports the identification of the tablets with covenant commandments, but it still supplies no link making those tablets a semantic component of Name.","Numbers 17 supports Aaron's rod as a sign validating the chosen priestly authority, but does not connect that sign to the definition of Name.","Exodus 20:7 identifies the Name as belonging to “the LORD thy God.” On the supplied evidence, misuse or empty invocation of God's Name is more direct than the entry's specialized claim that removal of any member of a three-part structure constitutes the offense.","Isaiah 4:1 is readily explained as women seeking the man's marital name, status, and protection. It supports household affiliation as one use of a name but not the universal threefold definition."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["It notices a genuine narrative chain linking God's Name, the temple, the ark, and the covenant in 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Kings 8.","It offers a coherent theological synthesis of the three objects listed in Hebrews 9:4.","It accounts meaningfully for household and covenantal belonging in Isaiah 4:1.","It correctly rejects the idea that a sacred name functions merely as a sound or magical formula."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["It preserves the explicit grammatical referent: the Name is the LORD's Name, while the temple, ark, and people bear or represent it.","It explains “house for my name” without converting the contents of the ark into a definition of the word Name.","It accommodates temple presence, covenant ownership, marital affiliation, reputation, and delegated authority as contextual expressions of the bearer's identity.","It requires fewer unstated transitions between Hebrews 9:4's inventory and the meaning of Name.","It fits Exodus 20:7 directly without making the command depend upon a three-element structure never mentioned there."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":["Second Samuel 6:2 and Exodus 20:7 explicitly present the Name as the Name of the LORD, whereas the entry identifies it as the covenant identity of a house. Treating God's personal Name as definitionally constituted by a house and its three elements reverses the texts' stated relation: the house and ark bear or serve God's Name; they are not said to generate or constitute it.","The temple is called a house “for” God's Name before 1 Kings 8:21 separately states that a place was set there for the ark. This distinction is straightforward if the temple honors and represents God, but conflicts with treating the ark's inventory as the actual substance of the Name.","Exodus 20:7 contains no reference to manna, tablets, priesthood, ark, or house. The entry's assertion that removal of any one of those elements is taking the Name in vain cannot be derived from the command without importing the disputed definition."],"comparative_winner":"COUNTER","decisive_sources":["2 Samuel 6:2","2 Samuel 7:13","1 Kings 8:20-21","Hebrews 9:4","Exodus 20:7","Isaiah 4:1"],"unresolved_objections":["The temple-ark-covenant sequence is sufficiently coherent to support a theological typology, even though it does not establish the entry's exact definition.","The broader common interpretation may itself be too expansive if treated as one invariant lexical meaning; context can emphasize presence, reputation, authority, or belonging differently.","The entry might be defensible as a specialized theological model for covenant-bearing communities rather than as the best general definition of the symbol Name."],"confidence":"high"}

support_scope.description: Support for the exact glossary BOOK ENTRY only, never for the supporting chapter as a whole.

book_secondary_elaborations.description: Secondary assertions actually printed in the glossary BOOK ENTRY; exclude chapter-only claims.

unsupported_glossary_assertions.description: Material assertions actually printed in the BOOK ENTRY that the evidence does not support. Must be empty for FULL and nonempty for CORE_ONLY.

chapter_only_objections.description: Objections to applications or arguments found only in the supporting chapter. Preserved for later chapter review and excluded from the glossary scope ruling.
